in_text_mentions: A five-year-old male patient with no significant medical or surgical history suffered a crush injury to his right hand from a soccer goal (approximately 60 kg). He presented to the emergency department 30 min after the incident, complaining of severe pain and deformity. On arrival, the physical examination revealed agitation, irritability, marked swelling, and deformity of the right hand, with restricted mobility due to pain and capillary refill of less than two seconds (Figure 1A).

Radiographic examination showed fractures of the second, third, fourth, and fifth metacarpals of the right hand with volar displacement. During the assessment period, the patient became irritable and experienced worsened pain with minimal finger movement (Figure 1B.1–B.3). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a radiographic AP view showing massive swelling of the hand. The figure is related to a case report on acute compartment syndrome in children, where swelling is a key indicator. B: Panel B is a radiographic lateral view showing massive swelling of the hand. This finding is consistent with the clinical context of acute compartment syndrome being monitored in this patient.
